install.title: Install guide: Windows app and phone pairing | SysWatch
install.description: Install SysWatch on Windows 10 or 11, get past the SmartScreen warning, choose Local, Cloud by DevLune or Tailscale, and pair your phone with one QR code.
install.h1: Install SysWatch and pair your phone
install.lead: SysWatch has two parts: the desktop app on the PC you want to watch, and the Android app on your phone. Install the desktop app first, then pair the phone.

blocks.p: SysWatch runs on Windows 10 and Windows 11, 64-bit. The installer is SysWatch_{version}_x64-setup.exe, about {size}. The phone app needs Android 7.0 or newer.
Every version and its release notes are on the SysWatch releases page on GitHub. To update, run the new installer over the old version: your pairing code and settings are kept.

steps: Windows SmartScreen may say “Windows protected your PC”. Choose More info, then Run anyway. The installer is not code signed yet.
Finish the installer and open SysWatch. It lives in the system tray.
Choose how your phone connects. The first run shows three cards: Local, Cloud by DevLune and Tailscale. Pick one, follow the steps it shows, and it ends on the pairing code.

blocks.p: SysWatch asks this the first time it opens and never asks for server details. You can change your answer later in Settings, where the same three choices appear as cards.

head: Compare
Local
Cloud by DevLune
Tailscale
rows: Tailscale on PC and phone, set up once
Through your own private Tailscale link

blocks.p: Not sure? Pick Local if the phone sits near the PC, and Cloud by DevLune if you check your PC from outside and do not want to set up Tailscale. Local and Tailscale need the latest version of both apps.

blocks.note: Local mode uses one port, 47800. The first time, Windows Firewall asks whether to allow SysWatch on private networks: choose Allow. Local mode is not encrypted, and the 6-character pairing code is the only lock, so use it on networks you trust: your home Wi-Fi, or Tailscale, which encrypts everything itself.

blocks.p: Want local speed away from home? The Tailscale guide takes about five minutes.

steps: Install SysWatch from Google Play and open it.
On the PC, open Pairing. The first run ends there by itself. A QR code and a 6-character code appear.
On the phone, tap Scan the code on your PC and point it at the QR code.

blocks.p: That is all. The QR code carries the mode, the address and the port, so there is nothing to type.

head: What you see
What to check
rows: Phone and PC are on the same Wi-Fi (not guest Wi-Fi, which isolates devices). Windows Firewall allowed SysWatch. The desktop app is running.
Local mode needs Tailscale away from home. See the Tailscale guide.
The PC made a new code. Open Pairing on the PC and scan again.
The desktop app is paused. Open it and press Resume.
Change the port in the desktop app's Settings, then scan the new QR code.

blocks.p: Still stuck? Open an issue on GitHub or ask on Discord.

tailscale.title: Tailscale guide: watch your PC from anywhere | SysWatch
tailscale.description: Set up Tailscale for SysWatch in about five minutes: a private, encrypted link between your phone and your Windows PC, so local mode works away from home.
tailscale.h1: Watch your PC from anywhere with Tailscale
tailscale.lead: Tailscale gives your PC and phone a private, encrypted link that works from anywhere, as if they were on the same Wi-Fi. With it, SysWatch local mode works away from home: instant updates, nothing sent through the SysWatch cloud.

blocks.p: Tailscale is a separate product with a free personal plan. SysWatch does not include it and does not need your Tailscale password.

steps: PC: install Tailscale from tailscale.com/download and sign in.
Phone: install Tailscale from Google Play and sign in with the same account.
Check that both show Connected in Tailscale. Each device now has an address that starts with 100.
SysWatch on the PC: choose Tailscale as the connection, on the first run or later in Settings. Tailscale runs on local mode, so a PC already set to Local works too.
Open Pairing. Under addresses you should see one labelled Tailscale.
SysWatch on the phone: scan the QR code.

blocks.p: Done. At home the phone uses your Wi-Fi address. Away from home, with Tailscale on, it switches to the Tailscale address by itself.

list: Keep Tailscale switched on on the phone when you are out. If it is off, SysWatch shows “PC not reachable” until you turn it back on.
On Android, Tailscale counts as the phone's VPN. Only one VPN can run at a time.
If you paired before installing Tailscale, scan the QR code again so the phone learns the Tailscale address.
No Tailscale address in the Pairing screen? Tailscale is not connected on the PC. Open it from the tray and sign in, then reopen Pairing.
The PC must be awake. Tailscale cannot reach a sleeping computer.

blocks.p: Installing SysWatch for the first time? Start with the install guide.

translate.title: Translate SysWatch into your language | SysWatch
translate.description: Add your language to SysWatch or fix a translation: copy en.xml, translate the text and open a pull request. A merged translation reaches the app by itself.
translate.lead: SysWatch speaks English, German, French, Spanish and Russian. You can add your language, or fix a wording in one that exists. No programming needed: it is one text file per language.

blocks.note: When a translation is merged, every SysWatch app picks it up by itself within a day, or at once from Settings, Language, Check now. No app update needed.

steps: Fork the SysWatch repository on GitHub (the Fork button at the top right of the GitHub page).

In the translations folder, copy en.xml and name the copy with your language code: hi.xml for Hindi, pt-BR.xml for Brazilian Portuguese, ja.xml for Japanese. The list of language codes has them in its first column.

steps.d: Translate the text between the tags. Leave everything inside the < > brackets alone.
steps.code:
<!-- English -->
<string name="pair_scan">Scan the code on your PC</string>

<!-- Your file -->
<string name="pair_scan">अपने पीसी पर कोड स्कैन करें</string>

steps: Open a pull request. A check runs by itself and tells you, in plain words, if anything needs fixing. Once it is green, the translation is reviewed and merged.

blocks.p: You do not have to finish in one go. Strings you leave out show in English, and the app tells people how complete a language is. But do not leave a string empty: delete the whole line instead.
Edit the file for that language (de.xml, fr.xml, es.xml, ru.xml), change the text and open a pull request. Say in a sentence why the new wording is better.

blocks.h2: The rules, all five of them

blocks.p: Things like %1$s and %2$d are slots the app fills in (a name, a number). Every one in the English must be in your text. You may move them to wherever your grammar wants them: that is why they are numbered.

blocks.code:
<string name="settings_paired_with">Paired with code %1$s</string>
<string name="settings_paired_with">Gekoppelt mit Code %1$s</string>

blocks.p: A real percent sign next to placeholders is written twice: %1$d%% shows as 47%.

blocks.h3: 2. Put a backslash before an apostrophe

blocks.p: l\'application, not l'application. Write & for &, and < for <.

blocks.h3: 3. Do not translate names and units

blocks.p: SysWatch, DevLune, CPU, GPU, RAM, Wi-Fi, Tailscale, Google Play, Windows, Android, and units such as MB, GB, GHz, °C stay as they are. The art standby faces (Horizon, Blocks, Bauhaus, Ink, Weave, Bloom, Type, Pixel) keep their names too.
English has two forms, one and other. If your language has more (Russian, Polish, Arabic…), add the forms it needs:

blocks.code:
<plurals name="settings_import_done">
    <item quantity="one">Импортировано %1$d правило.</item>
    <item quantity="few">Импортировано %1$d правила.</item>
    <item quantity="many">Импортировано %1$d правил.</item>
    <item quantity="other">Импортировано %1$d правила.</item>
</plurals>

blocks.p: This text sits on buttons and small cards on a phone. Prefer the word people actually use over the formal one. No long dashes: use a comma, a colon or a full stop.
The lines that start with <!-- in en.xml are notes for you: what a slot holds, or where the text appears. You do not need to keep them in your file.
One string is special: language_name is the name of your language, written in your language (Deutsch, Español, Русский, हिन्दी). That is what people see in the app's language list.
This step is optional. If you have Python, run this from the repository folder:
It prints ok or the exact strings to fix. The same check runs on your pull request.

list: languages.json in the translations folder is updated automatically. It is the list the app reads.

Apps check it once a day. A phone using your language downloads the new file, checks every string again on the device (a broken string is skipped and shown in English, so a mistake can never break the app), saves it, and shows it.
Languages that are not built into the app appear in the language list with a download mark. Popular ones get built in with the next app version.

blocks.p: Open an issue on GitHub or ask on Discord. Thank you for helping people use SysWatch in their own language.
